heading: Asset Allocation 101
body: Your mix of equity, debt, and gold matters more than which specific fund you pick within each. A simple 70/20/10 (equity/debt/gold) for a 25-year-old and a 40/50/10 for someone 5 years from retirement will usually beat a 'perfect' fund selection built on the wrong allocation for your age and goals.

heading: Why Index Funds Work
body: Over long periods, the majority of actively managed equity funds fail to beat their benchmark index after fees. An index fund guarantees you the market's return minus a tiny expense ratio (often under 0.3%) — for most investors, that's a very hard baseline to beat consistently.

heading: Rupee Cost Averaging, Explained
body: A fixed SIP amount buys more units when prices are low and fewer when prices are high, automatically. Over years, this smooths your average purchase cost without you ever having to predict market direction — the entire point is removing the guesswork, not timing it better.

heading: Debt Funds Aren't Risk-Free
body: Debt mutual funds carry interest-rate risk (prices fall when rates rise) and credit risk (the underlying bonds can default). A 'debt fund' label doesn't mean 'guaranteed return' — check the fund's average maturity and credit quality before assuming it behaves like a fixed deposit.

heading: International Diversification
body: Indian equity and the Indian rupee can both underperform at the same time. A small allocation (5-15%) to global index funds or ETFs gives you exposure to markets and currencies that don't always move with India's cycle — true diversification, not just more of the same risk.

heading: The Real Cost of Expense Ratios
body: A 1% difference in expense ratio sounds small, but compounded over 25 years on a growing SIP corpus, it can mean lakhs of rupees less in your final corpus. Always compare the Total Expense Ratio (TER) of similar fund categories before investing, not just past 1-year returns.

heading: Rebalancing, Not Reacting
body: Rebalancing means periodically moving your portfolio back to its target allocation (e.g. selling some equity after a rally to buy debt) — a mechanical, unemotional process. This is different from reacting to news, which usually means buying or selling based on a feeling, not a plan.

heading: What a Credit Score Actually Measures
body: Your CIBIL score mainly reflects repayment history, credit utilization, and credit mix/age — not your income or net worth. A high earner with maxed-out cards and missed payments can have a worse score than a modest earner who pays every EMI on time.

heading: Nominee vs Legal Heir
body: A nominee is simply the person authorized to receive your assets after you — they aren't automatically the legal owner unless they're also your legal heir under succession law. For larger assets, a will is still the clearest way to state who should ultimately own what.

heading: Why Goal-Based Investing Works
body: Tagging money to a specific goal (house down payment in 2031, retirement in 2050) forces a matching time horizon and risk level for that bucket. A single untagged 'investment pile' makes it much easier to raid long-term money for short-term wants.

heading: The Sequence-of-Returns Risk
body: Two investors with identical average returns over 30 years can end up with very different outcomes if one hits a market crash right before retirement and the other right after. This is why asset allocation usually gets more conservative as you approach the date you need the money.

heading: Direct vs Regular Mutual Fund Plans
body: Direct plans skip the distributor commission, so their expense ratio is lower and returns are correspondingly higher than the same fund's Regular plan — often by 0.5-1% a year. The trade-off is you manage the investment yourself instead of going through an advisor who earns that commission.

heading: Understanding Tax on Equity Gains
body: As of the current rules, equity mutual fund gains held over 1 year are taxed as long-term capital gains at a flat rate above an annual exemption threshold; gains under 1 year are taxed as short-term at a higher flat rate. Rules change — always check the current year's finance act before assuming last year's rates still apply.

heading: What a Fund's 'AUM' Tells You
body: Assets Under Management shows how much money a fund manages, not how good it is. A very large AUM in a small-cap fund can actually hurt performance, since the manager has less flexibility to move in and out of smaller, less liquid stocks without affecting prices.

heading: Why 'Past Performance' Disclaimers Matter
body: A fund's 5-star rating or last year's top returns usually reflect a specific market condition that favored its strategy — not a guarantee the same strategy will win again. Fund rankings rotate constantly; chasing last year's winner is one of the most common and costly investor mistakes.
